name: Rafael Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, governments or political parties. We don’t sell anything or campaign, and your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I became a junior manager of office services at a large insurance company last year, after doing the stationery orders for a long time; now six people expect me to decide what comes first. I'm 58 and have a bachelor's degree, but I still refer awkward staffing questions to my boss, and I've never used an AI tool. My wife works at a museum, our children are grown, and we have 13,800 saved against monthly spending of 4,600, including the mortgage and annual bills. I get the usual pay for this level, there are some other employers nearby, and I'd been hoping to stop at 66, though the pension figures haven't been checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good to stop talking about the office as if everybody's already left it. Somebody still has to make sure the new starters have passes and a place to sit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel our living was reasonably secure, even though I still find managing people uncomfortable. My 3,800 take-home and my wife's 1,700 cover our 4,600 spending, and the company has given me no sign that this job is ending. The 13,800 reserve is three months of total costs, not a reason to spend freely, but it's enough that one difficult meeting doesn't feel like disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the new-starter checklist and my boss's existing weekly staffing review through the first year. We'd continue putting the existing 900 monthly surplus into savings and paying the normal mortgage instalment. I'd leave any AI subscription alone, because I don't use the tools and a small improvement in somebody else's day isn't a reason to buy one myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about earning our living, with the ordinary discomfort of being new to management. I like a checklist that ends with a person getting a working door pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you ask your boss rather than decide alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If two staff wanted the same leave week and I couldn't see how to cover it fairly, I'd take the plan to him. I can say I'm still learning without making the team guess whether I've understood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does calm mean you'd spend the reserve on something nice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the reserve stays for trouble, and the 900 transfer is already our normal habit. We'd keep the small outings already in the budget rather than invent a reward for the news being less dramatic.

say: I'd welcome talking about the **office we have** rather than assuming everybody has already left.
I'd point to **new starters** who still need working passes and somewhere to sit.
think: I feel **financially secure** despite discomfort with managing, with both wages covering costs and no sign my post is ending.
Our **three-month reserve** cushions a difficult meeting without making unrestricted spending sensible.
do: Keep the **new-starter checklist** and existing weekly staffing review through the first year.
Continue the existing **900 monthly saving** and normal mortgage instalment without buying an AI subscription.
feel: **Calm about income**, while still uncomfortable with unfamiliar management decisions.
S0.quote: I like a checklist that ends with a person getting a working door pass.
fieldNote: His **calm** reflects stated job and household security, while junior management discomfort remains distinct from immediate income fear.
He explicitly calls the **900 transfer** an existing habit, so it is recorded as continuity rather than increased saving.

steps.text: Continue the new-starter checklist and existing weekly staffing review
Continue the existing 900 monthly savings transfer and normal mortgage payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say management should explain which office services it still wants people to provide. I'd rather hear an uncomfortable answer than be told to get excited about a programme I haven't used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordering, checking requests and allocating work are much of my day, so my junior post could be cut along with the clerical tasks. My wife has a wage and we have some cash, but I wouldn't be relaxed about finding work on the same pay. I could stay familiar for too long and discover the other local vacancies had gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at actual vacancies at two nearby large employers this month and apply for office-services work I understood, without insisting on a manager title. I'd use the ordinary application forms in my own time, ask about duties and hours, and resign only after a signed offer left at least 3,800 take-home after any extra travel. In the first year I'd keep the current checklists and weekly review while employed, and ask the employer for a plain explanation of any compulsory system change. I wouldn't claim I'd started learning AI when all I'd done was request the explanation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because I'd be trying to move before I was ready to want a move. Filling in a form is easier than explaining to my wife why I waited so long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use an AI-written application?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd write it myself and ask my daughter if she'd read it when she had time. I'd rather sound a little old-fashioned than submit an account of my work I hadn't written.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if an offer was below the pay floor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it wouldn't meet this plan, and I wouldn't resign unless my wife and I had separately agreed a lower-cost budget that actually worked. A lower wage printed on a contract doesn't reduce the mortgage by itself.

say: I'd ask which **office services** still need people rather than celebrate an unfamiliar programme.
I'd prefer an **uncomfortable explanation** to reassurance that doesn't describe actual staffing decisions.
think: My **junior post** could be cut because ordering, checking requests and allocating work dominate it.
I worry my **reluctance to change** could leave me too late for local vacancies at similar pay.
do: Check vacancies at **two local employers** and apply in personal time for office-services roles I understand.
Resign only after **signed terms** leave 3,800 take-home after extra travel, unless we separately agree a workable lower-cost household budget.
Keep current **checklists and reviews** while employed and request plain explanations of compulsory changes without claiming AI learning.
feel: **Anxious and reluctant**, trying to act before a move feels welcome.
S1.quote: A lower wage printed on a contract doesn't reduce the mortgage by itself.
fieldNote: His **applications** don't require a management title, but resignation depends on signed pay after travel or a separately agreed workable budget.
He distinguishes **asking for explanations** from actually learning AI, maintaining the resistant profile without denying the threat.

steps.text: Apply to office-services vacancies at two nearby employers in personal time
Resign only for signed terms meeting the 3,800 net-travel gate or agreed workable budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company can replace planning and checking before a machine can carry a desk upstairs. The 2031 robot date isn't the date I ought to put beside my own salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty in 2028 and I'd expect most of my office-services management work to go. My wife's 1,700 leaves a 2,900 monthly gap at today's 4,600 costs, and the reserve wouldn't fund that gap for five months. I don't know a pension payable at sixty, and her museum job could change as customer answering and later physical work are automated. I'd be awake wondering what I'd tell the mortgage lender.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our lender and insurer now what written permissions we'd need to rent the spare bedroom, and get the actual costs and local rules before offering it. I'd list a room only if my wife agreed and all required permissions were written down; I'd pay at most 150 for contract advice from one month's 900 surplus, leaving the 13,800 reserve untouched. In the first year after AGI, if my wage ended, I'd count room income only after an agreed written lodging contract and actual payment, less actual extra bills, tax and fees, with no tenant assumed today. I'd also ask the lender about temporary payment relief and seek eligible support if needed, without treating either application as money already received.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and uncomfortable about turning the room the children used into an advertisement. I can accept earning from a room more easily than I can accept pretending the room is already rented.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the room cover the whole gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't have a tenant, an agreed rent or the extra costs yet, so I can't say what it would cover. The enquiry is worth making, but I wouldn't tell my wife the mortgage was solved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the children for money first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask them to help us read the terms if they had time, not start with a standing payment from their wages. If we needed public help and qualified, I'd apply rather than quietly use up the reserve while keeping up appearances.

say: I'd explain that **planning and checking** can go before machines carry furniture.
I'd tell colleagues not to use the **robot date** as protection for a desk salary.
think: At **sixty**, I expect my management work to go without a known pension payable then.
Our **2,900 monthly gap** would exhaust the reserve inside five months, and my wife's museum income also faces change.
do: Confirm **room-rental rules** and written lender/insurer permissions before listing, with my wife's agreement.
Pay at most **150 for contract advice** from new monthly surplus, keeping 13,800 untouched; count only paid net rent under written terms.
Request **mortgage relief** and eligible support after wage loss, treating applications as requests rather than received money.
feel: **Alarmed and uncomfortable**, willing to enquire without pretending the spare room already earns.
S2.quote: I can accept earning from a room more easily than I can accept pretending the room is already rented.
fieldNote: His **room proposal** is conditional on household agreement, written permissions, local rules and an advice cap funded outside existing savings.
He assumes **no tenant or rent**, deducts actual costs before counting receipts and keeps mortgage relief separate from approval.

steps.text: Enquire about lodging rules; list only with written permissions and his wife’s agreement
Cap contract advice at 150 from surplus and count only received rent after actual costs
Request mortgage relief and eligible support after salary loss

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a reason to make the household less expensive, not a reason to buy five years of courses. I'd like to be able to show my wife one smaller bill rather than another brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 63 and still expect my management pay to end around 2031, before the 2034 robots. A lower mortgage could help, but equity in a home isn't the same as cash for food. I don't know whether pension income could begin then, so this is preparation for a loss, not a retirement date I've earned the right to announce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request written pension access dates and net amounts now and get the lender's terms for 400 monthly extra mortgage payments. I'd redirect 400 of our current 900 savings transfer only if there were no extra charges, my wife agreed, and the existing 13,800 stayed accessible, continuing 500 monthly into cash while both wages and costs held. I'd stop the overpayments if either wage fell or an unexpected bill required cash, whether before or after AGI. In the first year after AGI I'd use actual cash for any shortfall and seek eligible help if the pension figures and remaining income didn't cover costs; I wouldn't assume the loan was cleared or promise to stop working at 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing the pay, but more settled when the plan is a sum on the mortgage statement. I'd rather make one bill smaller than invent a safe new profession at 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not use the 13,800 to cut the mortgage immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because we'd still need cash if the washing machine failed or one wage stopped. I'd rather pay interest for a while than ask the lender to give us back money we'd already sent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your boss you planned to retire in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I've only said I expected the job to be exposed then. I'd need confirmed eligibility and net household income covering the real costs and unexpected bills before choosing any retirement date.

say: I'd use **five years** to reduce a household bill rather than collect course brochures.
I'd show my wife **actual debt progress** instead of promising a safe new career.
think: At **63**, I expect salary loss before robots despite any reduction in the mortgage.
Home **equity isn't cash**, and unconfirmed pension access prevents treating 2031 as a funded retirement date.
do: Request **pension figures** and mortgage terms before redirecting 400 of existing saving to debt, requiring no charges and my wife's agreement.
Retain **13,800 accessible**; save 500 monthly while wages and costs hold, stopping overpayments after either wage falls or unexpected cash needs.
Use **cash** for actual shortfalls after salary loss and seek eligible help if confirmed pension and other income don't cover costs.
feel: **Alarmed but more settled**, preferring visible debt reduction to an invented safe profession.
S3.quote: I'd rather make one bill smaller than invent a safe new profession at 63.
fieldNote: His **400 overpayment** reallocates the existing surplus, preserves accessible savings and has charge, household and income-change gates.
His **pension request** does not establish access, clear the loan or bring a funded retirement date into existence.

steps.text: Overpay 400 monthly only if charge-free, his wife agrees and 13,800 stays accessible
Stop overpayments after either wage falls or an unexpected bill requires accessible cash
Seek eligible help if confirmed income after job loss cannot cover costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the decade might allow a quiet finish for people our age, provided we stop confusing a birthday with a living. I'd still tell the children to make their own decisions rather than build a life around what I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68 when AGI arrived in 2036, two years after the 66 I'd hoped to stop at. That could work in our favour if pensions and costs matched, but I haven't established that yet. If my wife still needed her museum wage, robots around 2039 could matter to our income after I'd stopped. I'd feel less pressed than with 2028, not entitled to call the matter settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get written pension dates, net amounts and deductions now, then review them with my wife against actual spending once a year. I'd keep working and the ordinary savings transfer while both wages lasted, choosing a stopping date only if confirmed income covered costs and a separate amount for unexpected bills without relying on uncertain future wages. In the first year after AGI we'd compare actual income again and apply only for support we qualified for if the plan fell short. I wouldn't tell the children I'd committed to unpaid childcare until the retirement income and the time we could offer were both agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but able to imagine an end to work that didn't arrive as a surprise. I won't promise my grandchildren an afternoon of my wife's time without asking my wife.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire earlier than your hoped-for 66?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't make that change from an AI date alone. I'd need the same written income test for any earlier date, and I haven't got those figures now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why mention your wife's agreement about childcare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people ask a grandfather and then assume the grandmother is available too. We'd discuss which days, what travel cost and whether either of us was fit for it before saying yes; affection doesn't make every arrangement workable.

say: I'd say a **quiet finish** needs a living after work, rather than simply a birthday.
I'd encourage my **grown children** to choose for themselves instead of copying my working life.
think: At **68**, AGI could follow my hoped-for stopping age of 66, but matching pension income and costs is unconfirmed.
My wife's **museum wage** might still matter and face later robots, so I feel less pressed rather than secure.
do: Obtain **written pension figures** and review actual spending annually with my wife before choosing any stopping date.
Keep work and existing **saving** while both wages last; stop only with confirmed income covering costs and unexpected bills without uncertain wages.
Offer **grandchild care** only with funded retirement, agreed time, affordable travel and fitness; request eligible support if actual income falls short.
feel: **Anxious but less pressed**, imagining a planned end to work without committing his wife's time.
S4.quote: I won't promise my grandchildren an afternoon of my wife's time without asking my wife.
fieldNote: He retains his existing **hope of 66**, with no new early-retirement plan or assumed entitlement before written figures support a date.
His **childcare offer** remains conditional on funding, mutual agreement, travel and fitness rather than treating a partner's time as free capacity.

steps.text: Continue work and existing saving while both wages last pending confirmed affordable retirement
Agree any grandchild care only after retirement funding, shared time, travel and fitness checks
Apply for eligible support if actual post-AGI household income falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because sixty is too early to assume I can stop earning and too late to want another long climb. I'd want my actual notice and leaving terms, a proper explanation of pension access, and time to apply for work while still paid. My family would help me think, but I don't expect the children to fund a retirement I haven't funded myself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what people are protecting when they don't rush to learn the next thing. I'm protecting the bit of the day when I know what I'm doing, even though I understand that can become a trap. I don't think the company owes me the same desk forever, but I'd like a straight answer before the desk goes.

headlineQuote: I'm protecting the bit of the day when I know what I'm doing, even though I understand that can become a trap.
portrait: Rafael is **58**, a junior office-services manager with a bachelor's degree, still learning to prioritise six people's work.
He **never uses AI** and values familiar duties, accepting that his resistance can become a trap.
He and his **museum-worker wife** have grown children, a mortgage and three months of current household expenses saved.
His hoped-for **stopping age of 66** depends on unchecked pension figures, with room-rental enquiries and conditional mortgage repayment among his preparations.
biggestWorry: I fear **AGI by 2028** most because losing work at sixty wouldn't establish that I could stop earning.
whatWouldHelp: I need **written leaving terms**, pension access explained and time to apply for work while still paid.
